name: Chapter 1 - National accounts - Comprehensive MCQ Bank

questions.text: Modern GDP accounting as presented in the course was developed primarily:

options.a: in France in the  nineteenth century by Walras
options.b: after the 1970s oil shocks by Phillips and Solow
options.c: at the creation of the euro by the European Central Bank
options.d: in the United States in the 1930s by Simon Kuznets, with later refinement by Keynes

questions.text: One historical motivation for developing GDP measures was:

options.a: the need to measure the natural rate of unemployment during the 1970s
options.b: the need to calculate the money multiplier during the Great Depression
options.c: the need to set a nominal exchange-rate peg after the euro was created
options.d: the US Congress' desire to quantify the impact of the Great Depression

questions.text: According to the slides, GDP computation spread internationally especially:

options.a: after the creation of the World Trade Organization
options.b: after the 1979 oil shock only
options.c: after World War II, in the context following the Bretton-Woods conference
options.d: before World War I as part of the gold standard

questions.text: The statement that GDP is an "accounting construct" means that:

options.a: GDP is independent of all choices about what is included or how it is valued
options.b: GDP can only be measured with the income approach
options.c: its measured value depends on a set of statistical conventions and computation rules
options.d: GDP is a purely theoretical variable that is never measured

questions.text: If a statistical convention used to construct GDP changes, then, all else equal:

options.a: GDP becomes a stock variable instead of a flow variable
options.b: measured GDP growth can change even if the underlying economy has not changed in the same way
options.c: the expenditure and income approaches cease to be equivalent in theory
options.d: real production must necessarily change by the same amount

questions.text: Which is the course's basic output-side definition of GDP?

options.a: the value of all goods and services owned by residents at one instant in time
options.b: the value of all final goods and services produced within a country over a given period of time
options.c: the value of all primary and secondary incomes received anywhere in the world by residents
options.d: the value of all transactions involving domestic residents, whether intermediate or final

questions.text: Why must GDP use a value measure rather than simply adding physical quantities?

options.a: Because physical quantities are never observable.
options.b: Because an economy produces heterogeneous goods and services that need a common unit of aggregation.
options.c: Because using values automatically removes inflation.
options.d: Because only services can be measured in monetary units.

questions.text: The word "final" in the GDP definition is crucial mainly because it:

options.a: ensures that only durable goods enter GDP
options.b: prevents double counting of intermediate production stages
options.c: restricts GDP to goods bought by households
options.d: excludes all investment goods from GDP

questions.text: A medical consultation provided for payment is included in GDP because GDP:

options.a: classifies all services as intermediate production
options.b: includes only activities producing physical objects
options.c: includes both tangible goods and intangible services
options.d: includes only services and excludes goods

questions.text: The phrase "within a country" in GDP means that GDP is based on:

options.a: the nationality of the firm owner, regardless of where production occurs
options.b: the location of production, regardless of the producer's nationality
options.c: the currency in which the transaction is invoiced
options.d: the residence of the final consumer only

questions.text: GDP is a flow variable because it:

options.a: measures economic activity over a period such as a quarter or a year
options.b: cannot be compared across countries
options.c: is always expressed as a growth rate
options.d: measures wealth at a single instant

questions.text: Which of the following is a stock rather than a flow?

options.a: public debt measured on a given date
options.b: annual public deficit
options.c: household saving during a year

questions.text: A firm sells output for €500 and purchased €180 of intermediate goods and services used up in production. Its gross value added is:
Why would summing the revenues of all domestic firms generally overstate GDP?

options.a: Because exports would be counted negatively.
options.b: Because the value of intermediate inputs would be counted once when sold and again inside the value of final output.
options.c: Because depreciation would automatically be counted twice.

questions.text: Two economies produce exactly the same final bread, but one has more production stages. If GDP were measured by summing the value of every transaction, the economy with more stages would appear richer because of:

options.a: net income from abroad
options.b: double counting
options.c: purchasing power parity

questions.text: In the bread example, the value-added method gives the same GDP in the two economies because:

options.a: it ignores the final bread sale
options.b: it treats all intermediate transactions as exports
options.c: it uses only wages and excludes profits
options.d: it attributes to each stage only the additional value created at that stage

questions.text: Which alternative method is theoretically equivalent to summing value added across all domestic production stages?

options.a: sum every sale made by every firm
options.b: sum all intermediate purchases and subtract final sales
options.c: sum only the values of final goods and services

questions.text: Whether a product is intermediate or final depends primarily on:

options.a: whether it is expensive
options.b: whether it is produced by a corporation
options.c: how the product is used
options.d: the physical nature of the product

questions.text: Flour purchased by a bakery to produce bread for sale is:

options.a: an intermediate good
options.b: an export by definition
options.c: a final consumption good

questions.text: The same flour purchased by a household to bake bread for its own consumption is:

options.a: an intermediate good because it will be transformed
options.b: investment because it is durable
options.c: a final good

questions.text: A machine purchased by a manufacturing firm for repeated use in production is classified as:

options.a: an intermediate good because it helps produce other goods
options.b: a final investment good rather than an intermediate input
options.c: private consumption because it is purchased from another firm
options.d: an inventory only if it is used immediately

questions.text: A good that is produced but remains unsold at the end of the accounting period is treated as final output through:

options.a: net income from abroad
options.b: inventory investment
options.c: negative consumption

questions.text: An exported good is treated as final in domestic GDP accounting:

options.a: regardless of how the foreign buyer subsequently uses it
options.b: only if the foreign buyer is a household
options.c: only under a fixed exchange-rate regime
options.d: only if it is not transformed abroad

questions.text: A bottle of wine bought by a restaurant to serve to customers is:

options.a: always an export
options.b: fixed capital formation
options.c: an intermediate good for the restaurant

questions.text: A bottle of wine bought by a household for a dinner at home is:

options.a: a non-market output
options.b: an intermediate good because the household may combine it with food
options.c: a final consumption good

questions.text: Which cost is subtracted from a firm's revenue when calculating its value added?

options.a: employee wages
options.b: purchases of intermediate goods and services
options.c: the purchase price of a new machine used for several years

questions.text: A firm has zero economic profit because its revenue exactly covers all costs. Its value added is:

options.a: necessarily negative
options.b: not necessarily zero, because wages and other factor incomes are part of value added
options.c: necessarily zero
options.d: equal only to the value of intermediate inputs

questions.text: A firm that produces only intermediate goods:

options.a: creates value added only if it exports
options.b: can create positive value added if its output value exceeds the value of intermediate inputs it purchased
options.c: is excluded from GDP because none of its output is final
options.d: creates zero value added by definition

questions.text: How is non-market output of government and similar institutions valued in the production approach?

options.a: at zero because there is no market price
options.b: by adding social transfers paid by government
options.c: mainly at factor cost, using the cost of production such as wages rather than a market sale price
options.d: at the resale price of comparable private assets only

questions.text: A primary income is best defined as:

options.a: a capital gain on an existing asset
options.b: income generated by the creation and distribution of value added
options.c: any transfer received after taxes
options.d: income generated only by financial assets

questions.text: Which is part of labour primary income (compensation of employees)?

options.a: VAT collected on final purchases
options.b: unemployment benefits only
options.c: wages and salaries plus employers' social contributions

questions.text: Gross operating surplus includes:

options.a: only direct personal taxes
options.b: capital incomes such as interest, dividends, rent on fixed assets and retained profits
options.c: only unemployment benefits

questions.text: Gross mixed income is used especially for:

options.a: central banks only
options.b: foreign subsidiaries only
options.c: unincorporated businesses and independent workers, where labour and capital income are difficult to separate

questions.text: In the course notation, Gross Domestic Income is:

options.a: GDP minus exports plus imports
options.b: C + S only
options.c: Y_lab + Y_gop + T_ind

questions.text: Why are GDP by the production approach and GDI theoretically equal?

options.a: Because all value added created in production is distributed as primary income.
options.b: Because both count only household consumption.
options.c: Because GDI is defined as GDP minus depreciation.
options.d: Because both exclude taxes on production.

questions.text: In practice, measured GDP and GDI may differ slightly because of:

options.a: the use of different currencies within one country
options.b: the fact that wages are never included in GDI
options.c: a theoretical failure of the accounting identity

questions.text: Gross National Income differs from Gross Domestic Income because GNI is based on:

options.a: primary income received by fiscal residents, regardless of where it was generated
options.b: production located within the territory only
options.c: secondary transfers after taxation only
options.d: final consumption by domestic households only

questions.text: In a closed economy with no cross-border income flows:

options.a: GNI excludes labour income
options.b: GNI equals GDI
options.c: GNI is always greater than GDI
options.d: GDI equals NDI only if inflation is zero

questions.text: Net Income from Abroad (NIA) is:

options.a: secondary transfers received from abroad minus taxes
options.b: exports minus imports
options.c: primary income received by residents from abroad minus primary income generated domestically and received by foreign residents

questions.text: If residents earn €30 billion of primary income abroad while foreigners earn €22 billion of primary income domestically, then NIA equals:

options.a: €8 billion
options.b: −€8 billion
options.c: €52 billion

questions.text: If GDI is €500 billion and NIA is €12 billion, GNI is:

options.a: €512 billion
options.b: €12 billion
options.c: €488 billion

questions.text: A gross national-accounting variable differs from the corresponding net variable because the gross variable:

options.a: has not deducted fixed-capital depreciation
options.b: has not deducted imports
options.c: is measured at current rather than constant prices
options.d: includes secondary incomes while the net variable excludes them

questions.text: Net Domestic Income is obtained from Gross Domestic Income by:

options.a: subtracting depreciation of the fixed-capital stock
options.b: adding net exports
options.c: subtracting direct taxes and adding benefits

questions.text: Secondary income differs from primary income because secondary income:

options.a: arises from redistribution through taxes and transfers rather than directly from value-added creation
options.b: is always earned abroad
options.c: is part of GDP by the income approach

questions.text: Which item is a secondary income for a household?

options.a: wages paid for work
options.b: rental income from a productive asset
options.c: employer social contributions included in compensation

questions.text: Household disposable income is obtained from household primary income by:

options.a: subtracting transfers paid such as direct taxes and adding transfers received such as benefits
options.b: subtracting all indirect taxes only
options.c: adding depreciation and subtracting investment

questions.text: The expenditure identity for GDP is:

options.a: Y = C + I + G − X + M
options.b: Y = C + S + T + M
options.c: Y = C + I + G + X − M

questions.text: A household purchase of a new car is normally recorded in:

options.a: C, private consumption
options.b: I, because cars are durable
options.c: G, because cars use public roads
options.d: M only, regardless of where the car is produced

questions.text: A household purchase of a newly built house is recorded in:

options.a: not in GDP because land is involved
options.b: C because households consume housing services
options.c: I, gross fixed capital formation

questions.text: Renovation of an old residential building by a household is classified in the course as:

options.a: investment
options.b: a transfer
options.c: private consumption

questions.text: A firm's purchase of new production equipment is:

options.a: a secondary transfer
options.b: private consumption
options.c: gross fixed capital formation
options.d: an intermediate input fully subtracted from value added

questions.text: A positive change in inventories is counted as:

options.a: consumption
options.b: investment
options.c: negative exports

questions.text: A car is produced in year 1 and sold to a household in year 2 for €7,000. To keep the three GDP approaches consistent, year 1 includes:

options.a: +€7,000 of household consumption
options.b: −€7,000 of investment
options.c: no expenditure-side entry at all

questions.text: When that same €7,000 car is sold from inventory in year 2, the expenditure approach records:

options.a: +€7,000 in C and −€7,000 in inventory investment, for a net contribution of zero from the sale itself
options.c: +€7,000 in both C and I

questions.text: Government expenditure G includes:

options.a: only infrastructure investment
options.b: unemployment benefits as purchases of final services
options.c: government purchases of goods and services and wages paid by government

questions.text: Why are unemployment benefits not included in G?

options.a: They are subtracted as imports.
options.b: They are already included in exports.
options.c: They are counted as fixed capital formation.
options.d: They are transfers rather than government purchases of currently produced goods or services.

questions.text: Exports X are:

options.a: foreign goods purchased by domestic agents
options.b: primary incomes earned by residents abroad
options.c: domestically produced goods and services purchased by foreign agents

questions.text: Imports M are subtracted in the GDP expenditure identity because:

options.a: imports are never purchased by households
options.b: imports reduce domestic saving by exactly the import value
options.c: foreign production may already appear positively in C, I or G and must be removed from domestic GDP

questions.text: A Belgian household buys a €2,000 foreign-produced laptop. Ignoring taxes and margins, the direct accounting entries are:

options.a: +€2,000 in C and −€2,000 in M, giving zero direct contribution to Belgian GDP

questions.text: A Japanese tourist buys Belgian chocolates in Brussels for personal consumption. For Belgian GDP the purchase is:

options.a: an export X
options.b: domestic private consumption C
options.c: an import M

questions.text: Which activity is explicitly outside conventional GDP scope in the slides?

options.a: paid medical services
options.b: market production by a domestic firm
options.c: unpaid household work such as homemaking
options.d: government employee services valued at factor cost

questions.text: Illegal or undeclared market activity creates a GDP measurement problem because:

options.a: such activity never creates value added
options.b: it is automatically included through the CPI
options.c: some activity is not directly reported, although statistical estimates may be made
options.d: national accountants intentionally classify all illegal output as imports

questions.text: A polluting activity that creates €1 million of value added will, under standard GDP accounting:

options.a: raise GDP by €1 million even if it also creates substantial negative externalities
options.b: enter only if the pollution is later cleaned up
options.c: reduce GDP by the estimated pollution damage automatically
options.d: be excluded from GDP because pollution is harmful

questions.text: Why can pollution sometimes perversely raise measured GDP by more than the polluting production alone?

options.a: GDP adds the market value of depleted natural resources twice.
options.b: Negative externalities are entered as positive inventory changes.
options.c: Cleanup and health expenditures caused by the pollution can themselves generate measured production.
options.d: Pollution is recorded as an export.

questions.text: The course notes that conventional GDP does not properly reflect:

options.a: depletion of renewable but overexploited natural resources
options.b: employee compensation
options.c: exports of services

questions.text: A nominal variable is measured:

options.a: in current monetary units using prices prevailing when the variable is measured
options.b: using a fixed base-year price vector
options.c: only in physical units

questions.text: An increase in nominal GDP can be caused by:

options.a: higher quantities, higher prices, or both
options.b: higher quantities only
options.c: higher prices only

questions.text: The purpose of real GDP is to:

options.a: isolate changes in production volume from changes in prices
options.b: replace GDP with GNI
options.c: measure only government production
options.d: remove the need to value heterogeneous goods

questions.text: With real GDP at constant prices, all years are valued using:

options.a: the prices of one fixed reference year
options.b: each year's current prices
options.c: the prices of the immediately following year

questions.text: In the hot-dog/hamburger example with 2015 as base year, 2016 quantities are 150 hot dogs and 100 hamburgers, while 2015 prices are €1 and €2. Real GDP in 2016 is:
A key weakness of a fixed-base constant-price GDP series is that:

options.a: it makes nominal GDP impossible to compute
options.b: the weights can become increasingly unrepresentative as relative prices and economic structure change
options.c: it cannot be computed for the base year
options.d: it necessarily overstates inflation every year

questions.text: Real GDP measured at chained prices of the previous year differs from a fixed-base method because it:

options.a: re-estimates relative weights each year using the previous year's prices
options.b: uses current-year prices and therefore remains nominal
options.c: holds the composition of GDP fixed forever
options.d: never requires any reference year for expressing the final series

questions.text: The main advantage of chained real GDP highlighted in the course is that it:

options.a: eliminates statistical revisions
options.b: better accommodates structural changes and changes in relative prices over time
options.c: makes all international comparisons valid without PPP
options.d: always produces a higher growth rate

questions.text: To construct a chained real-GDP series, national accountants first calculate:

options.a: a single inflation rate from the CPI and apply it to all years
options.b: current-price GDP and divide by population only
options.c: year-to-year volume growth using previous-year prices, then chain those growth factors to a base-year level
options.d: GNI and subtract NIA in every year

questions.text: Except for the base year and typically the immediately following year, chained-price real GDP and fixed-base real GDP:

options.a: differ only if exports are nonzero
options.b: cannot both be expressed in the same monetary reference units
options.c: can differ because their weighting schemes differ
options.d: must be identical by accounting identity

questions.text: The GDP deflator is defined as:

options.a: real GDP divided by nominal GDP
options.b: CPI divided by nominal GDP
options.c: nominal GDP divided by real GDP for the same date and reference framework

questions.text: If nominal GDP is 840 and real GDP is 700, the GDP deflator in base-1 form is:
If the GDP deflator is expressed with base 100 and equals 125, this means that relative to the reference year:

options.a: the price level of final domestic output is 25% higher
options.b: real output is 25% higher
options.c: the CPI must also equal 125
options.d: nominal GDP is 125% higher regardless of quantities

questions.text: A GDP deflator of 171 in 2016 and 240 in 2017 implies a price growth factor from 2016 to 2017 of approximately:
GDP per capita is computed as:

options.a: GDP divided by the labour force
options.b: GDP divided by the number of inhabitants
options.c: GDP divided by the price level

questions.text: GDP per capita is interpreted in the slides as approximately:

options.a: the average household wealth stock
options.b: the average amount of primary income created per inhabitant
options.c: the average government transfer per resident
options.d: the median disposable income received by workers

questions.text: GNI per capita differs conceptually from GDP/GDI per capita because it focuses on:

options.a: primary income received by residents rather than primary income generated on the territory
options.b: only real variables
options.c: only household consumption

questions.text: For comparing material living standards over time within a country, the course recommends using:

options.a: gross investment per firm only
options.b: a real per-capita income measure rather than a nominal one
options.c: nominal GDP only

questions.text: A major problem with comparing nominal GDP per capita across countries using market exchange rates is that:

options.a: GDP cannot be expressed in a common currency
options.b: all countries use identical price levels
options.c: exchange rates are fixed by national accountants
options.d: exchange rates do not necessarily reflect differences in domestic price levels and purchasing power

questions.text: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) adjustments are designed primarily to:

options.a: replace real GDP with nominal GDP
options.b: turn GDP into a stock measure
options.c: convert incomes using relative purchasing power rather than market exchange rates alone

questions.text: The Big Mac index is an example of:

options.a: a simple PPP indicator based on comparing the price of a similar product across countries
options.b: a measure of unemployment duration
options.c: a GDP deflator based only on investment goods

questions.text: A limitation of the Big Mac index as a PPP measure is that:

options.a: it automatically double counts intermediate inputs
options.b: it uses only government goods
options.c: it cannot compare any two currencies
options.d: it relies on a single product rather than a broad representative basket

questions.text: (Select the incorrect answer) GDP/GDI per capita is useful as a welfare indicator because it:

options.a: fully captures environmental quality, leisure, inequality and all non-market activity
options.b: is synthetic and widely available
options.c: is often positively associated with several dimensions of material well-being
options.d: can be complemented with broader indicators such as the HDI

questions.text: Why should GDP per capita not be treated as a complete measure of welfare?

options.a: Because it is identical to the unemployment rate.
options.b: Because it excludes all services.
options.c: It omits or imperfectly captures dimensions such as distribution, non-market activity, externalities and other quality-of-life outcomes.
options.d: Because it cannot be measured in real terms.

questions.text: The Human Development Index is presented as useful because it:

options.a: is simply another name for PPP-adjusted GDP
options.b: measures only the GDP deflator
options.c: replaces all national-accounting identities
options.d: supplements income information with other dimensions of human development

questions.text: A domestic firm buys €40 of imported intermediate inputs and produces a final good sold domestically for €100. Ignoring taxes, the firm's domestic value added is:

A domestic firm buys a new €30 domestic machine and €20 of domestic raw materials, then sells final output for €90. In the production approach, the firm's own value added from the final-output production is:

options.a: €60, because only the machine is subtracted
options.b: €70, because only the €20 raw materials are intermediate inputs
options.c: €40, because both the machine and raw materials are intermediate

questions.text: A municipality buys new printers for its administration. Under the course classification, the most appropriate interpretation is:

options.a: they are excluded because government has no output
options.b: they are household consumption
options.c: the printers are inputs used by government production rather than household final consumption

questions.text: A company buys chocolates to give to clients as part of its business activity. In the national-accounting logic used in the tutorial, the chocolates are:

options.a: private consumption
options.b: gross fixed capital formation
options.c: an intermediate business purchase

questions.text: If a Dutch company holds a seminar in a Belgian hotel, the Belgian hotel service is:

options.a: a Belgian import
options.b: an intermediate good excluded from Belgian GDP
options.c: Belgian household consumption

questions.text: Suppose nominal GDP grows by 12% while real GDP grows by 5%. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.a: Prices must have fallen by 7%.
options.b: The GDP deflator must be unchanged.
options.c: Part of nominal GDP growth reflects an increase in the aggregate price level of final output.

questions.text: A country's nominal GDP is unchanged, but its GDP deflator rises. Holding the accounting identities together, real GDP must:

options.a: rise
options.b: equal GNI regardless of NIA
options.c: fall

questions.text: If a country's population grows faster than its real GDP, real GDP per capita:

options.a: cannot be determined even with those two growth rates
options.b: falls
options.c: rises

questions.text: A resident of Belgium earns wages by working in Luxembourg. Relative to Belgian GDI and GNI, this wage:

options.a: raises Belgian GNI but not Belgian GDI
options.b: raises both because residence and territory are irrelevant
options.c: raises neither because cross-border wages are secondary income
options.d: raises Belgian GDI but not Belgian GNI

questions.text: A French resident works in Belgium and earns wages from Belgian production. Relative to Belgian accounts, the wage contributes to:

options.a: Belgian GDI but not Belgian GNI
options.b: Belgian secondary income only
options.c: Belgian GNI but not Belgian GDI
